limits.title: Limitations
limits.synthetic: This is a demo site with synthetic data. Nothing here is a real measurement.
limits.estimate: Every number is an estimate from satellite data, not an engineering survey.
limits.provisional: NISAR products are provisional (first data from 17 June 2026); validated products are planned for the end of 2026.
limits.gap: There is no NISAR data from 27 July to 10 August 2026 (instrument gap).
limits.tide: Radar and optical images are taken at different tides; on flat, muddy banks the water edge moves by tens of metres with the tide.
limits.rate: “Years until the river arrives” assumes the bank keeps moving at its 1988–2026 average speed. Rivers change course; the range shown is from the spread of the measurements only.
limits.motion: Ground movement is not used at this site: only {{pct}} % of the land kept a stable radar signal over the season (30 % needed).
limits.population: People counts come from WorldPop estimates and OpenStreetMap buildings, which miss some homes.
limits.bangla: Bangla text has not yet been checked by a native speaker.

about.intro: The Last Safe Home tracks river-bank erosion and flooding in coastal Bangladesh with radar from the NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite and 38 years of Landsat images, and turns them into a Home Risk Score and an estimated range of years until the river arrives — for any point you click.
about.challenge: Built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, challenge “Dancing with the SARs”.

home.badge: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Dancing with the SARs
home.question: When will the river reach this house?
home.lead: In coastal Bangladesh the rivers take a little more land every year. We use radar from the NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite and 38 years of Landsat images to show, for any home, how fast the river bank is moving and roughly how many years are left.
home.sceneAlt: Illustration: sunrise over a river in Bangladesh. A family's house stands on a crumbling bank, a boat passes, and a dashed line far out in the water shows where the bank was in 1988.
home.storyIntro: Millions of people in Bangladesh live beside its rivers. The river is their life — and their biggest risk.
home.givesBody: Fish, rich soil for rice, boats to the market and evenings by the water. Life on the char is hard work, but it is home.
home.takesBody: Every monsoon the bank breaks a little more. Fields, schools and houses fall into the water, and families move again — some of them many times.
home.unknownBody: Monsoon clouds hide the river from ordinary satellite photos, and land surveys rarely reach the chars. Families decide to stay or to move on instinct.
home.numEroded: km² of land taken by the river since 1988
home.numBuildings: buildings within 500 m of today's bank
home.numFastest: metres a year — the fastest-moving bank
home.numPasses: NISAR radar passes in the 2026 monsoon
home.numbersNote: From our maps of real NISAR and Landsat data. Estimates, not an engineering survey.
home.howTitle: How it works, in four steps
home.step1Body: NISAR sends microwaves to the ground every 12 days — day or night, rain or shine. Calm water looks dark and land looks bright, so we can map the river on every pass.
home.step2Body: Landsat photos since 1988 show where the bank was in each dry season.
home.step3Body: Every 100 m along the shore we draw a line across the bank and measure how many metres it moved each year.
home.step4Body: Distance to the bank ÷ speed of the bank = years until the river may arrive. Add how often the place flooded, and you get a Home Risk Score from 0 to 100.
home.f1Body: Its score, the years until the river may arrive, distance to the bank and flood frequency.
home.f2Body: Step through every NISAR radar pass of 2026, through the clouds.
home.f3Body: How often each place was under water this monsoon.
home.f4Body: Land lost each year, and buildings and people by risk class.
home.f5Body: Swipe to see how much land has gone in one generation.
home.f6Body: Every word in Bangla, and a one-page report to take to the union parishad.
home.dataTitle: The data we use, and how
home.dataIntro: All of it is free and open. Here is what each source tells us.
home.nisarWhat: A new radar satellite, launched in 2025, that sees the ground through clouds every 12 days.
home.nisarHow: Water and land on each 2026 pass, how often places flood, and where the bank is today.
home.landsatWhat: Satellite photos of the Earth taken since the 1970s.
home.landsatHow: The river bank every five years from 1988 to 2026, to measure how fast it moves.
home.s2How: To check that our radar water map is right.
home.osmWhat: A free map of the world, made by volunteers.
home.osmHow: Buildings, schools and roads near the bank.
home.worldpopWhat: The estimated number of people in every 100 m square.
home.worldpopHow: How many people live in each risk class.
home.geobWhat: Official borders of unions and upazilas.
home.toolsLine: Built with open-source tools — Python (NumPy, rasterio, scikit-image), FastAPI, React and MapLibre. The code is MIT-licensed.
home.teamIntro: We are four students from Khulna, Bangladesh — a few hours from the rivers on this map. We built The Last Safe Home for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Khulna local event) because here, river erosion is not a news story: it is our neighbours' lives.
home.ctaTitle: Find out when the river may reach a home
home.ctaBody: Open the map, click a house, and get a number you can take to the union parishad.
home.footerDisclaimer: Every number is an estimate from satellite data, not an engineering survey.
